results.title: github.com/sainp7/flow
highlights:
A Java-Streams / .NET-LINQ-style functional collection pipeline for Go whose
intermediate operations **preserve your concrete stream type**.
...
Every fluent stream/collection library — Go's
jucardi/go-streams (a separate,
third-party library this project takes inspiration from), Java's `Stream `,
LINQ in C# — has intermediate operations return the **base** stream type. That's
fine until you extend the base with your own domain methods. The moment you chain
through a single built-in operation, your concrete type is gone:

```go
// A naive base: Filter returns the base interface, not your type.
type IStream[T any] interface {
    Filter(f func(T) bool) IStream[T]
}
...
NewUserStream(users).
    ActiveOnly().            // *UserStream — fine
    Filter(hasVerifiedEmail). // returns IStream[User] — concrete type LOST
    AdultsOnly()              // compile error: IStream[User] has no method AdultsOnly
```

This is the classic **"self type" problem**. A shared base method can only name
the base type (chain breaks) or `any` (every caller must type-assert). There was
no third option in Go — until 1.26.
...
## The fix: `Stream[T, Self]`

Go 1.26 lifted the restriction that a generic type may not appear in its own
constraint. That lets the stream interface name the concrete type as a type
parameter, so **every intermediate operation returns `Self`** — your exact type —
and the chain stays concretely typed with zero assertions:

```go
type Stream[T any, Self Stream[T, Self]] interface {
    Filter(f func(T) bool) Self
    Sort(f func(T, T) int, desc ...bool) Self
    // ...
}
```

`Self` is constrained by `Stream[T, Self]`, which itself mentions `Self` — the
recursive form that requires Go 1.26. (The release-note canonical example is
`type Adder[A Adder[A]] interface { Add(A) A }`.)

| | Naive base | flow |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Intermediate op returns | `IStream[T]` (base) | `Self` (your type) |
| Chain a base op then a domain method | **compile error** | ✅ compiles |
| Runtime cost of the safety | — | **none** (see benchmarks) |
...
Defining your own stream takes three things: embed `flow.Base` with a
pointer to your own type, wire the self-pointer once with `Init`, and add your
domain methods.

```go
type User struct {
    Name     string
    Active   bool
    Age      int
    Verified bool
}

type UserStream struct {
    flow.Base[User, *UserStream]
}

func NewUserStream(users []User) *UserStream {
    s := &UserStream{}
    return s.Init(s, users) // the single line of "self" wiring
}

// Domain methods — not part of the base library — return *UserStream because
// Filter does.
func (s *UserStream) ActiveOnly() *UserStream {
    return s.Filter(func(u User) bool { return u.Active })
}

func (s *UserStream) AdultsOnly() *UserStream {
    return s.Filter(func(u User) bool { return u.Age >= 18 })
}
```

Now custom and built-in operations interleave freely, and `*UserStream` survives
every hop — this chain compiles and runs:

```go
result := NewUserStream(users).
    ActiveOnly().             // custom method
    Filter(hasVerifiedEmail). // base method — Self preserved
    AdultsOnly().             // custom method again, still available
    Sort(byName).             // base method again
    ToArray()
```
...
Why the `Init` call? Go's generics give you type-level self-reference, but not
automatic runtime self-binding — `Init(self, source)` records the concrete
pointer once so promoted base methods can return it. It's a known, expected part
of the pattern, not a workaround.
...
A Go method cannot introduce a type parameter beyond those on its receiver. So a
cross-type map (`From` → a *different* `To`) or a cross-type reduction can't be a
chained method — they are standalone generic functions instead. (This mirrors how
jucardi/go-streams handles the same language constraint; it's not an oversight.)
...
`Reduce`/`Sum`/`Min`/`Max` are same-type or already-typed and could in principle
be methods, but stay standalone functions for a consistent aggregate API.
Same-type mapping needs no new type parameter, so `Map` *is* a chained method.

results.title: cmd/compile: generic method returning parameterized self-type causes "instantiation cycle" when return type wraps receiver type parameter
highlights:
# cmd/compile: generic method returning parameterized self-type causes "instantiation cycle" when return type wraps receiver type parameter
...
A generic method whose return type wraps the receiver's type parameter in a
composite struct triggers a "instantiation cycle" compile error when that
return type must itself satisfy the same interface.
...
func (*Impl[T]) seal()              {}
func (i *Impl[T]) Self() *IFace[T]  { var x IFace[T] = i; return &x }
...
// OK: standalone function
func ZipFnT, U any *Impl[Pair[T, U]] {
    return &Impl[Pair[T, U]]{}
}

// BROKEN: same signature as a method
func (i *Impl[T]) ZipU any *Impl[Pair[T, U]] {
    return &Impl[Pair[T, U]]{}
}
...
```
./prog.go:8:11: instantiation cycle:
	./prog.go:24:41: T instantiated as Pair[T, U]
...
Successful compilation. The method signature `func (i *Impl[T]) ZipU any *Impl[Pair[T, U]]`
is well-typed, and the standalone-function equivalent `ZipFn` compiles without
error. The compiler should accept the method form as well.
...
This prevents legitimate fluent/chained API patterns in generic container
libraries. For example, a generic `Option[T]` type with an interface-implementing
chain wrapper cannot express `Zip` as a method:

```go
// Option[T] interface includes:   Into() *Chain[T]

// Works: standalone
func ZipOptionT, U any Option[Pair[T, U]]  // OK

// Broken: method on Chain — same instantiation cycle
func (c *Chain[T]) ZipU any *Chain[Pair[T, U]]          // CYCLE
```
...
When the compiler verifies that `*Impl[Pair[T, U]]` satisfies `IFace[Pair[T, U]]`,
it needs to instantiate `Impl[Pair[T, U]]`'s method set. Within that set, the
return type of `Zip[U]` is again `*Impl[Pair[T, U]]`, which triggers re-verification
of the same interface satisfaction check before the first one completes.

The cycle is in **method-set verification**, not in the type system itself.
The standalone function has no receiver and therefore no method set to verify,
which is why it doesn't trigger the cycle.
...
):
>
...
A[A[T]]) {}
...
> This is unrelated to "re-verification of the same interface satisfaction check". Rather the error comes from the monomorphization checker which tests whether code for generic functions/methods can be monomorphized.
> 
> This is a deliberate restriction in the Go compiler to prevent an infinite loop during the compilation process.
> 
> To understand why this code cannot be monomorphized, one has to look at how Go handles generic functions versus generic methods when generating concrete code (stenciling).
> 
> Monomorphization is the process where the compiler takes generic code and generates a concrete version of it for every specific type used in your program. When a generic type is instantiated, the compiler generates all the methods for that specific instantiation (it cannot generate methods on the fly).
> 
> If one were to declare a variable of type `A[int]`, here is the chain reaction the compiler would be forced to follow:
> 
> 1. The code contains the declaration `var x A[int]`.
> 2. The compiler instantiates the type `A[int]`.
> 3. To complete `A[int]`, the compiler must generate all methods for `A[int]`, which includes `m`.
> 4. The method signature becomes: `func (A[int]) m(A[A[int]])`.
> 5. Because the type `A[A[int]]` is now part of a compiled method signature, the compiler must also ensure `A[A[int]]` is fully formed and generate its methods.
> 6. The compiler instantiates `A[A[int]]`.
> 7. It generates the methods for `A[A[int]]`, making the method signature: `func (A[A[int]]) m(A[A[A[int]]])`.
> 8. This requires instantiating `A[A[A[int]]]`, which requires `A[A[A[A[int]]]]`, and so on, forever.
> 
> If the compiler allowed this, the compilation process would never finish. The error `T instantiated as A[T]` is the compiler's circuit breaker catching this expanding recursive pattern.
> 
> The function `func fT any {}` does not cause this error. In this case, the compiler needs to generate only one concrete version of `f` where `T` is `int`. It does not automatically generate an `f` for `A[int]` unless the code explicitly makes such as call elsewhere. Here's a (further simplified) example illustrating this point. This function `f` is fine (playground):
> 
> ```go
> type A[T any] struct{}
> 
> func fT any {}
> ```
> 
> But this version isn't (playground):
> 
> ```go
> type A[T any] struct{}
> 
> func fT any { f(A[T]{}) } // ERROR: T instantiated as A[T]
> ```
> 
> for the same reason as why there is an error for the method example. The call `f(A[T]{})` forces a new version of the function `f` to be generated, which would force yet another one to be generated, forever.
> 
> In short, the Go compiler cannot translate your code into a finite amount of code and it is not equipped to generate code on the fly (which may perhaps terminate, depending on the structure of the code).
> 
> Thus, this is working as intended.
...
> That simplified reproducer seems relevant to #80172, but I think it ignores an important aspect of *this* report, which is that the method in question is generic.
> 
> Here's a short reproducer that actually has the generic method property: https://go.dev/play/p/5y8wkZPKJi9
> 
> ```go
> type Tup[A, B any] struct{}
> 
> func ConsA, B any Tup[A, B] { return Tup[A, B]{} }
> 
> func (t Tup[A, B]) PrependX any Tup[X, Tup[A, B]] {
> return Cons(x, t)
> }
> ```
> 
> Why would the compiler have to recursively instantiate a generic method? Is it actually assuming that if it needs to instantiate `Tup[X, Y].Prepend[W]`, then it's also going to need (due to the return type) `Tup[W, Tup[X, Y]].Prepend[W]` and so on down the line, even though that method can't be used in an interface (and therefore only needs to be generated if it's actually statically called)? Or, put another way, is it generating `Prepend[W]` for every `Tup[A, B]` instantiation due to the stenciling mechanics, even if it's only actually needed for `Tup[X, Y]`? If so, given that generic methods already cannot implement interfaces, couldn't the generic methods be represented internally as top-level functions instead of stenciled?
> 
> I just started poking around with generic parameters on methods, and ran into this within a couple of hours. It's surprising behavior - it works just fine with a top-level method, so it's very strange that what feels like syntactic sugar (and it does make for much simpler callsites in many cases) has this odd restriction.

results.title: github.com/JayceChant/go-stream
highlights:
A Go 1.27 generics implementation of the Java Stream API — built on the newly introduced **generic methods** feature, enabling natural, fluent stream processing in native Go for the first time:
...
Before Go 1.27, methods could not declare their own type parameters, so chained APIs like `Map[U]` could only be written as package-level functions (`stream.Map(s, f)`) with no fluent chaining. With generic methods, methods on `Stream[T]` can carry their own type parameters, enabling fully chained declarations with static type migration along the pipeline.
...
- **Generic methods**: method-level type parameters such as `Map[U]`/`Zip[U, R]`/`Collect[A, R]` let element types migrate statically along the pipeline
...
: reads top-down ... pipeline order,
...
Mirrors Java's primitive streams (`IntStream`/`LongStream`) — not for boxing avoidance (Go generics have zero boxing), but for **constraint narrowing**: `NumberStream[N Number]` embeds `Stream[N]`, moving the element constraint into the wrapper's own type parameter. This sidesteps the Go 1.27 rule that methods cannot constrain the receiver's existing type parameter, so element-constrained APIs become chainable methods (`stream.Range(0, 100).Sum()` in one line):
...
Narrowed method surface: element-preserving intermediates (`Filter`/`Peek`/`TakeWhile`/`DropWhile`/`Limit`/`Skip`/`Reverse`), natural-order ops (`Sorted()`/`StableSorted()`/`Distinct()`), flags/lifecycle (`Parallel`/`Sequential`/`Unordered`/`OnClose`), and narrowed terminals (`Sum()`/`Avg()`/`Min()`/`Max()`/`Contains()`). Non-overridden promoted methods keep Stream semantics: type-migrating operators (`Map[U]`/`Zip`/`Scan`) return `*Stream`, value terminals (`ToSlice`/`Count`/`Collect`) work directly. Both bridges copy the handle and mark the source consumed — one-shot semantics, second bridge panics.
...

results.title: Go compiler doesn't allow pointer-to-receiver methods on an interface struct field value when that interface type is defined with a generic parameter. · Issue #63447 · golang/go
results.author: g-talbot
highlights:
## Go compiler doesn't allow pointer-to-receiver methods on an interface struct field value when that interface type is defined with a generic parameter.
...
Discovered an issue where, when a generic interface is specified as a struct type parameter, a value of that interface type in the struct, though it requires a pointer-to-concrete-implementation, will not allow the concrete implementations to have pointer-to-receiver typed methods. Discussed this in [this comment](https://github.com/golang/go/issues/49030#issuecomment-1752009899), but figured it was worth a bug report.

I came across this when having a similar problem, but the suggestion given in that issue does not allow items of generic type embedded as fields to have methods that allow the embedded field to be modified. When you name the field, you cannot have methods on that type with pointer receiver. This means that you cannot write the following (toy example):
...
func main() {
	var lockable LockableValue[IntegerValue]
	lockable.value = &IntegerValue{}

	lockable.LockedFromString("1234")
	lockable.LockedIncrement()
	fmt.Println ... value=", lockable.ToString())
}
...
[Does not compile](https://go.dev/play/p/5p6Y3gEiMZe). ./prog.go:38:29: IntegerValue does not satisfy SomeValue (method FromString has pointer receiver). If we [modify the code](https://go.dev/play/p/Q3i0ZK-OC-i) to make all of the methods have a non-pointer receiver, then `FromString()` and `Increment()` methods cannot make changes to the `value` field on the line that says `lockable.value.Increment()`:
...
```
	lockable.value = &IntegerValue{}
```

So the field is indeed an interface which points to an implementation. If I omit this line, the program crashes with a segfault due to a null pointer exception.

I can understand where embedding the type directly is disallowed, for the reasons given, however if using the type as a named field as "value SomeValue" above is the solution, what is the means to allow the embedded type to be modifiable with methods that have pointer receiver?

I ask this because I indeed have cases where I can abstract functionality over a set of implementations in an orthogonal manner using this technique, except for the pointer-to-receiver issue. I would like the generic type (`LockableValue` in this case) to be able to call methods on the field (`value` in this case)

I believe this to be an actual compiler bug, as the `value` field of `LockableValue` above is indeed a pointer-to-interface (the `lockable.value = &IntegerValue{}` is required for the program to not crash), but the compiler won't allow e.g. `IntegerValue` to have pointer-to-receiver methods.
...
I expect the first ... , where `IntegerValue` has pointer-to-receiver methods, to compile, and for this program to output `value= 1235`
...
Did not compile, and when I changed the offending methods to not take pointer-to-receiver, the program output `value= 0`.
...
> working as expected, you need a pointer to the type
